prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Late in the cold night wakened, and heard wind, And lay with eyes closed and silent, knowing These words how bodiless they are, this darkness Empty under my roof and the panes rattling Roughed by wind. And so lay and imagined Somewhere far off black seas heavy-shouldered Plunging on sand and the ebb off-streaming and Thunder forever. So lying bethought me, friend, What traffic ghouls have, or this be legend, In low inland hollows of the earth, under Shade of moon, the night moaning, and bitter frost; And feared the riches of my bones, long given Into this earth, should tumble to their hands. No girl or ghost beside me, and I lonely, Remembering gardens, lilac scent, or twilight Descending late in summer on that town, I lay and found my years departed from me, And feared the cold bed and the wind, absurdly Alone with silence and the trick of tears.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Late, And, These

outputs.L1:
Late in the cold night, I awakened and heard the wind.  
I lay silent, my eyes closed, knowing  
How bodiless these words are—this darkness,  
Empty beneath my roof, and the panes rattling,  
Roughened by the wind. And so I lay, imagining  
Somewhere far off black seas, heavy-shouldered,  
Plunging upon the sand, the ebb streaming away, and  
Thunder everlasting. Thus lying, I wondered, friend,  
What traffic ghouls might have—if this be legend—  
In the low inland hollows of the earth, beneath  
The moon’s shadow, the night moaning, and bitter frost;  
And I feared that the riches of my bones, long given  
Into this earth, might tumble into their hands.  
With no girl or ghost beside me, and lonely,  
Remembering gardens, the scent of lilacs, or twilight  
Descending late in summer upon that town,  
I lay and found my years departed from me,  
And feared the cold bed and the wind—absurdly  
Alone with silence and the trick of tears.
outputs.L2:
Awake deep in the freezing night, I listened  
To gusts outside, lying still with shut eyes, aware  
How insubstantial language seemed, how vacant  
The dark beneath my roof, while window glass  
Shook in the harsh air. Motionless, I pictured  
Distant, ink-black oceans lifting their great weight,  
Breaking upon beaches, then draining backward  
With an endless roar. As I remained there, friend,  
I wondered whether grave-robbers truly barter—  
Or whether it is only an old tale—  
In shallow hollows far within the land, beneath  
The moon’s dim cover, while night groans and frost bites;  
And I was frightened that the treasure of my bones,  
Long buried in the soil, might fall into their keeping.  
With neither woman nor spirit at my side, alone,  
I recalled gardens, the perfume of lilacs, and dusk  
Arriving slowly over that town in summertime.  
There I rested, discovering my years had slipped away,  
And irrationally dreaded the chilled bed and the wind,  
Left only with stillness and tears’ familiar deception.
outputs.L3:
The speaker awakens in the middle of a cold, windy night and lies motionless in bed, surrounded by deep darkness. As he listens to the storm, his imagination carries him toward distant black seas, where waves crash endlessly against a desolate shore. His thoughts then descend beneath the earth to ghoulish creatures waiting in the shadows, and he shudders at the possibility that, after death, his own buried bones might fall into their hands.

With no companion beside him to offer warmth or comfort, he turns instead to memories of the past. He recalls fragrant gardens, blooming lilacs, and the gentle light of summer twilight—images of beauty that sharply contrast with the bleakness of the present night. These memories remind him of the years that have vanished and of all that time has taken from him. Alone in his cold bed, he is left to confront his loneliness, his fear of death, and the sorrow of irretrievable loss, until his grief finally gives way to tears.
outputs.L4:
Awake on a cold, windy night, the speaker finds that sleep offers no refuge from unsettling thoughts. The darkness transforms the world into a threatening imaginative landscape filled with vast seas, ghostly figures, and intimations of death. These images reflect an inner state of profound loneliness: separated from warmth, companionship, and the ordinary distractions of daylight, the speaker becomes intensely conscious of physical vulnerability and of the silence that surrounds an isolated life.

Against this bleak setting, memories of summer briefly return. Summer represents warmth, vitality, pleasure, and a time when life seemed abundant and secure. Yet these recollections provide little lasting comfort. Their very brightness emphasizes how completely that season has passed, just as youth and earlier happiness have passed. The contrast between remembered warmth and the present cold makes time’s movement feel especially cruel. What has vanished cannot be recovered, and memory preserves the past only while confirming its absence.

The speaker’s thoughts then turn toward mortality and the eventual fate of the body. Death is not treated as a distant abstraction but as a physical reality: the living body will decay, disappear, or become something strange and unrecognizable. The imagined ghouls embody this fear, giving a disturbing shape to anxieties about what happens when personal identity can no longer be sustained. Such visions suggest that death threatens not only life itself but also the familiar sense of being an individual housed within a recognizable body.

Aging intensifies these fears because it gradually removes the protections that once kept them at a distance. Physical strength declines, relationships may be lost, and comforting memories become reminders of irreversible change. Isolation strips away reassurance, leaving the speaker alone with the knowledge that time moves in only one direction. The night therefore becomes more than a temporary period of sleeplessness: it represents the emotional darkness in which the speaker confronts the limits of human existence.

Ultimately, the cold, the wind, the imagined supernatural figures, and the memories of summer all express the same underlying anxiety. The speaker longs for warmth and continuity but recognizes that neither can be preserved forever. The result is a poignant meditation on loneliness, aging, and death, marked by an acute awareness that every moment passes beyond recovery. In the silence of the night, mortality becomes immediate, and the loss of time feels both deeply personal and universally human.
outputs.L5: It was late, and the streets had fallen silent. These were the hours when forgotten memories returned—softly, without warning—asking to be heard. She stood by the window, watching the city lights fade, and wondered whether every ending was simply a beginning waiting for morning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about waking alone on a cold, windy night and contemplating death, memory, and loneliness.
counterfactuals.output:
I wake to the window trembling  
in its frame,  
the wind worrying the roof  
like an animal that has forgotten  
how to enter.

Beside me, the sheet is cold—  
a pale country  
no one has crossed for years.

Night has taken everything  
but the small red eye of the clock,  
its numbers changing  
without mercy,  
without sound.

I think of death  
not as a door  
but as a room slowly emptied:  
first the chairs,  
then the photographs,  
then the dust where sunlight  
once lay down.

How strange  
that memory warms nothing.

I summon a face  
and find only gestures—  
a hand lifting a cup,  
hair blown across a mouth,  
someone turning at the gate  
as if called.

Was it winter then?  
Was I the one who left?

The wind answers  
in all the voices it has stolen,  
pressing them thin  
against the glass.

I lie still, listening,  
the last awake thing  
in a world of locked houses,  
and feel my heart  
keep its lonely appointment—

knock after knock  
at an unopened door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a melancholic first-person poem in an early modernist style, using imagery of rattling windows, distant black seas, graves, ghosts, lilacs, and summer twilight.
counterfactuals.output:
At summer twilight the windows rattle  
though no wind troubles the lilacs;  
their pale clusters lean at the sill  
like hands that have forgotten blessing.

I sit alone in the failing room,  
counting each pane’s thin cry,  
and think of the distant black seas  
where my lost years drift without stars.

Beneath the hill, the graves grow cool.  
Ghosts move softly among the stones,  
wearing the faces I once loved,  
speaking my name as if it were rain.

I would answer—but evening deepens,  
and the house draws close around me.  
Only the lilacs breathe in the dark,  
only the windows rattle on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an eerie, reflective poem addressed briefly to a “friend,” contrasting a bitter nocturnal landscape with nostalgic memories of gardens and a vanished town.
counterfactuals.output:
Friend, the night has salted every field;  
black branches scrape the moon like bone.  
A wind moves through the roofless mill,  
counting the names cut from the stone.

Do you remember the gardens there—  
pear blossom, mint, the drowsing bees,  
the fountain holding noonlight still,  
green doors half-hidden by the trees?

The town is gone. Its roads run pale  
beneath the weeds, then disappear.  
Only the bell, though no bell hangs,  
tolls once across the frozen mere.

I walk where lamplight used to bloom  
in windows warm with bread and rain.  
Friend, if you dream of that lost place,  
do not wake me there again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a somber literary poem with irregular line breaks and elevated diction about aging alone in bed, haunted by thoughts of burial, ghouls, silence, and lost summers.
counterfactuals.output:
**Nocturne in the Last Room**

The bed has learned my shape—  
a shallow grave rehearsed in linen,  
where each old bone lies down  
with the obedience of rain.

Beyond the glass,  
the moon whitens the garden into ash.

I hear no footfall in the hall,  
no cup set softly by a beloved hand;  
only the clock, that little iron ghoul,  
gnawing the dark  
                                        one second at a time.

How sumptuous the summers were—  
their orchards loud with bees,  
their rivers bearing our bright bodies  
as though death were a country  
not yet invented.

Now silence enters without knocking.  
It sits beside me,  
draws the cover to my chin,  
and speaks in the sepulchral tongue  
of earth upon wood,  
of roots insinuating themselves  
through the elegant vacancy of ribs.

I imagine the burial:  
rain stippling the black umbrellas,  
a spade’s dull benediction,  
my name already weathering  
on the stone.

And underneath—what ghouls attend?  
Not claw nor fang, perhaps,  
but memories famished into phantoms:  
your laughter at the lake,  
the green flare of July,  
my own young face turning away  
before I knew  
how little remained to turn toward.

The night deepens.

In this enormous bed  
I am the last warm province,  
besieged by cold—  
still listening for summer  
to ascend the stairs,

though all the stairs are gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
